title: Current and voltage
keyIdea: Current is how fast charge flows round a circuit, measured in amps with an ammeter in the loop. Voltage (potential difference) is the energy each charge gives up or gains, measured in volts with a voltmeter across a part.

kid: A circuit is a loop. Tiny charges flow all the way round it. The battery gives each charge a push and some energy.
Current is how much charge goes past a point each second. We measure it in amps (A) with an ammeter. It sits in the loop.
Voltage is how much energy each charge drops off at a part, like a bulb. We measure it in volts (V) with a voltmeter. It sits across the part, on its own side loop.
A bulb does not use up current. The same current comes out as goes in. The bulb takes energy, not charge.
adult: Current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q ÷ t, so 1 A means 1 coulomb per second. In a single loop it is the same at every point, which is why an ammeter can go anywhere in series.
Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge: V = E ÷ Q, so 1 V means 1 joule per coulomb. Around a series loop the voltages across the parts add up to the battery's voltage.

Ammeters have almost no resistance and go in series; voltmeters have a very high resistance and go in parallel. In metal wires the charges that move are electrons, drifting the opposite way to the conventional current arrow.

familyTip: Look on a phone charger or a battery: it gives the voltage (for example 5 V or 1.5 V). Look at a kettle plug label for the current (for example 13 A). Talk about which one is a push and which one is a flow.

practice.prompt: An ammeter before a bulb reads 0.4 A. What does an ammeter just after the bulb read?
practice.hint: Is charge used up in a bulb?
practice.explain: 0.4 A. In a single loop the current is the same everywhere. The bulb takes energy from the charges, not the charges themselves.

practice.prompt: A battery is made of {n} cells in a row, each 1.5 V. What is the battery's voltage?
practice.hint: Cells in a row add their voltages.

practice.prompt: How should a voltmeter be connected to measure the voltage of a bulb?
choices: In the loop next to the bulb (in series)
practice.hint: It compares the energy before and after the part.
practice.explain: Across the bulb, in parallel. It measures the energy each charge gives up between the two sides of the bulb.

practice.prompt: A {v} V battery lights {b} identical bulbs in one loop. What is the voltage across each bulb?
practice.hint: The bulbs share the battery's voltage equally.

pool.prompt: Two identical bulbs in one loop each have {h} V across them. What is the battery's voltage?
pool.hint: Around a loop the voltages add up to the battery's.

pool.prompt: What does a current of 2 A mean?
choices: 2 coulombs of charge pass each second
pool.hint: Current is a rate of flow.
pool.explain: 1 amp = 1 coulomb per second, so 2 A means 2 coulombs of charge flow past each second.

pool.prompt: Sam puts a voltmeter into the loop, in series with a bulb. What happens?
choices: The bulb goes out, because a voltmeter hardly lets current through
pool.hint: A voltmeter has a very high resistance.
pool.explain: A voltmeter has a huge resistance, so in the loop it almost stops the current. The bulb goes out.

pool.prompt: An ammeter in a loop reads {=a/10} A. A second ammeter, after two bulbs, is added. What does it read, in A?
pool.hint: In one loop, is current shared out or the same everywhere?
pool.explain: The same: {=a/10} A. Current is the same at every point in a single loop.

pool.prompt: You add a second identical bulb to a one-bulb loop with the same battery. What happens?
choices: Both bulbs are dimmer: each gets half the voltage and less current flows
pool.hint: The two bulbs share the battery's push.
pool.explain: The voltage is shared, and with more resistance the current falls, so both bulbs are dimmer.

pool.prompt: Which is the best description of voltage?
choices: The energy given to or taken from each unit of charge
How much charge flows each second
pool.hint: Its unit, the volt, is a joule per coulomb.
pool.explain: Voltage (potential difference) is energy per unit charge: 1 V = 1 J per coulomb.

pool.prompt: A torch needs {v} V. Each cell gives 1.5 V. How many cells must be put in a row?

visual.caption: Current only flows round a complete loop of conductors. Put each object in the gap: does the bulb light?

lab.caption: Flagship lab: the circuit bench. Move the meters, add cells and bulbs, and watch charge and energy flow.
